intro.title:
Video platform
Udemy / Netflix-style
intro.subtitle: Upload gigabytes, transcode asynchronously, stream from the CDN: no application server ever touches a video byte.

cues.cap: Designing a video platform in the style of Udemy or Netflix, flow by flow.

Three flows: uploading, which is rare but huge; transcoding, which is heavy and asynchronous; and watching, which is constant, around 70 Gbps. Let's follow one lesson from the instructor's laptop to the student's player.
cues.say: Three flows: uploading, which is rare but huge; transcoding, which is heavy and asynchronous; and watching, which is constant, around seventy gigabits per second. Let's follow one lesson from the instructor's laptop to the student's player.

scenes.title: Six services, three flows, zero video bytes

steps.cap: The upload path: the browser asks API Gateway and Upload Service for a presigned URL, Course / Metadata Service records the video in Postgres, and the file goes straight to the Raw Bucket in S3.
steps.say: The upload path: the browser asks A P I Gateway and Upload Service for a presigned U R L, Course Metadata Service records the video in Postgres, and the file goes straight to the Raw Bucket in S three.
steps.title: Upload path
steps.note: Thin requests only. The 4 GB file travels browser → S3; our servers never see its bytes.

steps.cap: The transcoding path is asynchronous: an S3 event lands in SQS or Kafka, Transcoding Workers pull jobs, run FFmpeg in parallel and write HLS segments to the Processed Bucket.
steps.say: The transcoding path is asynchronous: an S three event lands in S Q S or Kafka, Transcoding Workers pull jobs, run F F m peg in parallel and write H L S segments to the Processed Bucket.
steps.title: Transcoding path
steps.note: The instructor waits only until uploaded, never until ready. The queue depth drives the size of the worker pool.

steps.cap: The watch path never passes through the application servers: a signed URL, manifest and segments from the CDN, a key from DRM License Service, and playback progress written to Redis.
steps.say: The watch path never passes through the application servers: a signed U R L, manifest and segments from the C D N, a key from D R M License Service, and playback progress written to Redis.
steps.title: Watch path
steps.note: 70 Gbps of segments come from CDN edges. The app servers answer only who may watch what and where you stopped.

steps.cap: The instructor picks a 4 GB file and clicks Upload. The browser sends POST /videos/upload with the title and size; API Gateway authenticates the user and forwards the call over gRPC to Upload Service.
steps.say: The instructor picks a four gigabyte file and clicks Upload. The browser sends post slash videos slash upload with the title and size; A P I Gateway authenticates the user and forwards the call over G R P C to Upload Service.
steps.title: Client → API Gateway → Upload Service
steps.code:
POST /videos/upload
Authorization: Bearer …
{ course: 'c_31', title: 'Lesson 12',
  size: 4294967296 }

→ gRPC Upload.Start(user, course, title, size)
steps.note: Only metadata travels here: a few hundred bytes, not the file.

steps.cap: Upload Service creates the video record through Course / Metadata Service, stored in Postgres with state UPLOADING. The state machine of the video starts here.
steps.say: Upload Service creates the video record through Course Metadata Service, stored in Postgres with state uploading. The state machine of the video starts here.

steps.cap: Then it asks S3 for a presigned multipart URL: a temporary link that lets exactly this client write exactly this key in the Raw Bucket for the next few minutes.
steps.say: Then it asks S three for a presigned multipart U R L: a temporary link that lets exactly this client write exactly this key in the Raw Bucket for the next few minutes.
steps.code:
s3.createMultipartUpload(
  { Bucket: 'raw', Key: 'v_812.mp4' })
→ uploadId
presign PUT raw/v_812.mp4
  ?partNumber=N&uploadId=…  expires: 900 s
steps.note: The signature binds bucket, key and expiry, so the link is useless for any other object.

steps.cap: The URL goes back to the browser. From here on our servers are out of the loop.
steps.say: The U R L goes back to the browser. From here on our servers are out of the loop.
steps.title: Upload Service → Client

steps.cap: The browser uploads the file in 8 MB parts directly to S3 over HTTPS. If the connection drops, it resumes from the last confirmed part: a resumable upload that costs us no bandwidth at all.
steps.say: The browser uploads the file in eight megabyte parts directly to S three over H T T P S. If the connection drops, it resumes from the last confirmed part: a resumable upload that costs us no bandwidth at all.
steps.title: Client → Raw Bucket (S3)
steps.code:
PUT raw/v_812.mp4?partNumber=37&uploadId=…
→ 200  ETag: "a9f3…"
…
CompleteMultipartUpload(parts: 1 … 512)

steps.cap: When the last part lands, S3 itself emits an ObjectCreated event into the video-uploaded queue, and the record moves to UPLOADED. The instructor sees 'processing', because the UI reads exactly that field.
steps.say: When the last part lands, S three itself emits an Object Created event into the video uploaded queue, and the record moves to uploaded. The instructor sees processing, because the U I reads exactly that field.
steps.title: S3 → queue

steps.cap: The first free Transcoding Worker pulls the message. Pull, not push: a worker takes a job only when it has a free slot, so 1 000 simultaneous uploads do not crash the pool, they simply wait in the queue.
steps.say: The first free Transcoding Worker pulls the message. Pull, not push: a worker takes a job only when it has a free slot, so a thousand simultaneous uploads do not crash the pool, they simply wait in the queue.
steps.code:
receiveMessage(video-uploaded, max: 1)
visibilityTimeout: 900 s
-- redelivered if the worker dies
steps.note: The pool autoscales on queue depth, not on CPU. Paid uploads get their own queue so free ones cannot starve them.

steps.cap: It first checks whether the output objects already exist in the Processed Bucket. If the queue delivered the message twice, the worker finishes without doing any work: the consumer is idempotent.
steps.title: Idempotency check
steps.code:
HEAD processed/v_812/master.m3u8
→ 200  already done: ack, exit
→ 404  start the job
steps.note: Queues are at-least-once; the worker, not the queue, guarantees that work happens once.

steps.cap: It reads the original, cuts it into one-to-two-minute chunks on keyframe boundaries without re-encoding, and publishes one job per chunk and resolution back to the queue: 60 chunks times 4 resolutions is 240 independent jobs across the whole pool.
steps.say: It reads the original, cuts it into one to two minute chunks on keyframe boundaries without re-encoding, and publishes one job per chunk and resolution back to the queue: sixty chunks times four resolutions is two hundred forty independent jobs across the whole pool.
steps.title: Split and fan out
steps.code:
ffmpeg -i raw/v_812.mp4 -c copy -f segment \
  -segment_time 90 chunk_%03d.mp4
→ 60 chunks × { 1080p, 720p, 480p, 360p }
→ 240 messages → video-uploaded

steps.cap: Every worker encodes its chunk with FFmpeg, writes the result to the Processed Bucket under a deterministic key, and increments a counter in Redis.
steps.say: Every worker encodes its chunk with F F m peg, writes the result to the Processed Bucket under a deterministic key, and increments a counter in Redis.
steps.title: Encode one chunk
steps.code:
ffmpeg -i chunk_017.mp4 -vf scale=-2:720 \
  -c:v libx264 -hls_time 6 …
PUT processed/v_812/720p/chunk_017/seg_*.ts
INCR transcode:v_812 → 239
steps.note: Deterministic keys make a retried chunk overwrite itself instead of creating a duplicate.

steps.cap: The worker that sees the counter reach 240 does the fan-in: it stitches the segments, writes the .m3u8 manifests and the thumbnails.
steps.say: The worker that sees the counter reach two hundred forty does the fan-in: it stitches the segments, writes the M three U eight manifests and the thumbnails.
steps.title: Fan-in
steps.code:
INCR transcode:v_812 → 240   ✓ last one
master.m3u8 → 1080p.m3u8, 720p.m3u8,
               480p.m3u8, 360p.m3u8
thumbnails/*.jpg, subtitles.vtt

steps.cap: Then it calls Course / Metadata Service over gRPC: READY. The lesson appears in the course.
steps.say: Then it calls Course Metadata Service over G R P C: ready. The lesson appears in the course.
steps.code:
gRPC Metadata.SetState(v_812, 'READY',
  manifest: 'processed/v_812/master.m3u8')

UPDATE videos SET state = 'READY'
 WHERE id = 'v_812';

steps.cap: If an encoder fails, the job is retried with backoff up to N times, then goes to a dead-letter queue with an alarm and the video becomes FAILED, without the instructor uploading the file again.
steps.say: If an encoder fails, the job is retried with backoff up to N times, then goes to a dead letter queue with an alarm and the video becomes failed, without the instructor uploading the file again.
steps.title: A chunk fails
steps.note: The original is still in the Raw Bucket, so a fix means replay the DLQ, not a new upload.

scenes.title: Watching: signed URL, CDN, DRM, progress

steps.cap: The student opens the lesson. The player asks for the video: GET /videos/:id goes through API Gateway to Course / Metadata Service, which checks in Postgres that the student bought the course.
steps.say: The student opens the lesson. The player asks for the video: get slash videos slash I D goes through A P I Gateway to Course Metadata Service, which checks in Postgres that the student bought the course.
steps.title: Client → API Gateway → Metadata Service
steps.code:
GET /videos/v_812
Authorization: Bearer …
→ gRPC Metadata.GetPlayback(
    user: 'u_42', video: 'v_812')
SELECT 1 FROM enrollments
 WHERE user_id = 'u_42'
   AND course_id = 'c_31';

steps.cap: It returns a signed URL to the manifest, valid for a few minutes. The signature travels inside the URL; the CDN will check it at the edge.
steps.say: It returns a signed U R L to the manifest, valid for a few minutes. The signature travels inside the U R L; the C D N will check it at the edge.
steps.title: Metadata Service → Client
steps.code:
200 OK
{ manifest: 'https://cdn.example.com/
    v_812/master.m3u8?exp=1760342400
    &sig=8f1c…',
  drm: 'https://drm.example.com/license' }

steps.cap: The player fetches the manifest from the CDN, then the segments one by one. The edge verifies the signature; on a miss it pulls the segment once from the Processed Bucket and serves everyone else from its cache.
steps.say: The player fetches the manifest from the C D N, then the segments one by one. The edge verifies the signature; on a miss it pulls the segment once from the Processed Bucket and serves everyone else from its cache.
steps.title: Client → CDN → Processed Bucket
steps.code:
GET /v_812/master.m3u8?exp=…&sig=…
GET /v_812/1080p/seg_001.ts
→ edge HIT 97 %
→ MISS: GET s3://processed/v_812/…
        then cache at the edge

steps.cap: The player measures the connection itself and picks 1080p or 480p for the next chunk: adaptive bitrate, decided on the client, invisible to the servers.
steps.say: The player measures the connection itself and picks ten eighty p or four eighty p for the next chunk: adaptive bitrate, decided on the client, invisible to the servers.
steps.title: Adaptive bitrate
steps.code:
throughput 8 Mbps → 1080p/seg_041.ts
throughput 2 Mbps → 480p/seg_042.ts
buffer < 10 s → step down one rung

steps.cap: Because the segments are encrypted, the player asks DRM License Service for a key. The service asks Course / Metadata Service over gRPC whether the right is still valid and returns the key: Widevine or FairPlay.
steps.say: Because the segments are encrypted, the player asks D R M License Service for a key. The service asks Course Metadata Service over G R P C whether the right is still valid and returns the key: Widevine or FairPlay.
steps.title: Client → DRM License Service → Metadata

steps.cap: Every 5 to 10 seconds the player sends PUT /progress. API Gateway forwards it over gRPC to Progress Service, which writes the position to Redis immediately.
steps.say: Every five to ten seconds the player sends put slash progress. A P I Gateway forwards it over G R P C to Progress Service, which writes the position to Redis immediately.
steps.title: Progress: write-behind
steps.code:
PUT /progress { video: 'v_812', pos: 742 }
→ gRPC Progress.Set(
    user: 'u_42', video: 'v_812', pos: 742)
SET progress:u_42:v_812 742

steps.cap: A periodic job flushes the positions to Postgres in batches, so another device resumes from the same spot and the database never sees 100 000 writes per second.
steps.say: A periodic job flushes the positions to Postgres in batches, so another device resumes from the same spot and the database never sees a hundred thousand writes per second.
steps.title: Redis → Postgres, in batches
steps.code:
every 10 s:
SCAN progress:*  → 1 000 keys per batch
UPDATE progress SET pos = v.pos
  FROM (VALUES ('u_42','v_812',742), …)
    AS v(u, vid, pos)
 WHERE progress.user_id = v.u
   AND progress.video_id = v.vid;
steps.note: Losing a few seconds of progress on a Redis failover is acceptable; losing the database to 100k writes/s is not.

recap.title: What to say in the interview
recap.closing:
Thin requests.
Not a single video byte.

items.text: Presigned URL: the file goes browser → S3, never through us
items.cap: To sum up. A presigned URL sends the file from the browser straight to S3; our servers never carry video bytes.
items.say: To sum up. A presigned U R L sends the file from the browser straight to S three; our servers never carry video bytes.

items.text: S3 event → queue → workers that pull, not push
items.cap: An S3 event feeds a queue, and workers pull jobs at their own pace: the queue absorbs the spike.
items.say: An S three event feeds a queue, and workers pull jobs at their own pace: the queue absorbs the spike.

items.text: Fan-out per chunk and resolution, fan-in on a Redis counter, DLQ
items.cap: Transcoding fans out per chunk and resolution and fans in on a Redis counter, with idempotent workers and a dead-letter queue.

items.text: Signed URL + CDN + DRM: the watch path bypasses the app servers
items.cap: Watching is a signed URL, segments from the CDN and a key from DRM; the application servers only answer thin requests.
items.say: Watching is a signed U R L, segments from the C D N and a key from D R M; the application servers only answer thin requests.

items.text: Progress write-behind: Redis first, Postgres in batches
items.cap: And progress is write-behind: Redis first, Postgres in batches. Thin requests, not a single video byte.
